cards.title: Sip before you're thirsty
cards.summary: Thirst means you're already behind on fluids.
cards.body: By the time you feel thirsty, you've typically already lost 1-2% of your body water. Sipping steadily through the day — rather than chugging large amounts at once — keeps energy and focus more stable, especially around workouts.

cards.title: Electrolytes matter after sweat
cards.summary: Water alone isn't always enough after a hard session.
cards.body: Heavy sweating flushes out sodium and potassium along with water. After long or hot workouts, a pinch of salt or an electrolyte tablet in your water helps your body actually retain the fluid you're drinking instead of running straight through you.

cards.title: Protein spread through the day
cards.summary: Even distribution beats one big serving.
cards.body: Muscle protein synthesis responds best to protein spaced across 3-4 meals rather than one large dose at dinner. Aim for a palm-sized portion of protein at each meal instead of saving it all for one sitting.

cards.title: Carbs are training fuel, not the enemy
cards.summary: Timing carbs around workouts improves performance.
cards.body: Carbohydrates refill the glycogen your muscles burn during exercise. A small carb-containing snack 60-90 minutes before a run, and some carbs afterward, helps you perform better and recover faster — regardless of your overall goal.

cards.title: Cadence over stride length
cards.body: Many new runners overstride, landing heavily out in front of the body. Aiming for a slightly quicker cadence (around 170-180 steps/min) naturally shortens your stride and softens impact on your knees and shins.

cards.title: Easy days should feel easy
cards.summary: Most of your running should be conversational pace.
cards.body: A common mistake is running every session near max effort. Keeping the majority of your runs at a pace where you could hold a conversation builds your aerobic base without piling up fatigue that blocks real progress.

cards.title: Sleep is when adaptation happens
cards.summary: Training breaks you down; sleep builds you back up.
cards.body: The physical improvements you're chasing — more endurance, more strength — largely happen during deep sleep, not during the workout itself. Consistently under-sleeping blunts these gains no matter how hard you train.

cards.title: Soreness isn't a scoreboard
cards.summary: You don't need to be sore to have had a good session.
cards.body: Muscle soreness is a sign of unfamiliar or increased stress, not a reliable measure of workout quality. Consistent, moderate training that leaves you a little tired — not wrecked — tends to produce better long-term results.
